This investigation employs an active flame technique to represent turbulent jet flames reacting to acoustic excitation, formulated within a CFD framework using a partially linearized treatment. These outcomes indicate the technique's robustness for modeling high-temperature, chemically reactive turbulent jets under extreme conditions.

We have recently developed a computational framework capable of simulating the thermodynamic behaviors of 2D lattice fluids with arbitrary site configurations. Using this framework, we investigated a scenario where two distinct lattice gases exist under varying temperatures and pressure, with inter-site interactions and individual site volumes. Our findings reveal thermodynamic clustering behaviors that mirror real-world systems, even though no explicit interaction mechanisms were included between sites in our computational model.

To better understand the physics driving this clustering, we analyzed the thermodynamic and structural properties of a one-dimensional analogy. By comparing our 1D results against a computationally derived clustering metric based strictly on geometric topology—considering only the connectivity and arrangement of sites in two dimensions—we explored how this inherent spatial layout may decouple physical phenomena from specific inter-site interaction models. This study confirms that the lattice topology itself can be a significant factor in the observed clustering of multi-site fluids.

If Earth contains neutrinos and ultralight dark matter in equilibrium via mutual "bath" states, the neutrino half-lives shrink due to enhanced phase space. Consequently, even minuscule dark neutrino densities—suppressible by the encountered neutrino effects—can cause orders-of-magnitude enhancements in $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay rates. This mechanism tightly constrains the interaction between neutrinos and ultralight dark matter, influencing cosmology, the cosmic microwave background, the formation of large-scale structures, the evolution of stars and white dwarfs, as well as the densities of the solar neutrino and supernovae. As a result, the "thermally averaged" neutrino density may exceed the critical density by many orders of magnitude while remaining consistent with current cosmological data. However, combining cosmological constraints with those from $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay indicates that the true half-free neutrino density cannot exceed the critical density by more than approximately ten orders of magnitude. These findings have significant implications for the proposed detection of the Cosmic Neutrino Background by PTOLEMY.

The theory of magnetic catalysis suggests that the spin-sensitive ultra-high-energy photons emitted by astrophysical sources, which interact negligibly with external magnetic fields, could have their effective magnetic permeability significantly enhanced by the Earth's or Sun's ambient field. To test this, we performed spin-flip calculations using extended, more precise, and fully relativistic formulae for photon absorption cross-sections within highly inhomogeneous solar magnetic environments. We found that for photons with energies exceeding 10^19 eV traveling perpendicular to the solar equator, the catalytic reduction in their mean free path occurs already at field catalyzing lower values of 10^-13 G. Furthermore, the catalyzing effect becomes negligible for photons of any orientation at even higher threshold intensities exceeding 10^-9 G. However, for photons exceeding 10^19 eV moving parallel to the solar equator, strong catalysis requires much higher ambient field intensity exceeding 10^-7 G. Although no such ultra-high magnetic field regions have yet been definitively observed in the atmosphere, transient phenomena such as coronal mass ejections could plausibly generate them. We advance a four-dimensional classical framework of nonlocal gravitation, designed so that effects arising from mass distributions elsewhere can be modeled with the same surface and bulk formalism used in frictionless nonlocal solid and surface mechanics. Within the formalism, a constitutive connection is established to relate a nonlocal essential tetrad to the spatial distribution of gravity mass. This tetrad serves as a measure of how gravity mass transports energy and momentum. The surface and bulk surface nonlocal variational principles are employed to derive the corresponding laws of motion. The connection between this newly presented formalism and other approaches in gravity physics is also discussed. Specifically, we demonstrate how specific choices of the constitutive connection can cause the derived equations to match a subset of Einstein's field equations. Also, we show that the formalism is capable of representing a uniform acceleration that matches the value of local gravity.

Distributed data storage systems utilizing distribution, where data is replicated across remote servers accessible via uniform interfaces, represent a proven technology. Among these, Redis is a prominent example implements its network layer with an single write-order model to ensure consistency. However, the current solution in this area, called "enter-write," forces applications to implement synchronization logic independently to handle global halts in the N-1 manner to fit this linear model, a burden that could be better handled at the data layer. To provide a consistent optional ordering model in which programs do not need implementing application-level quorums for global pauses in the distributed environment we call Eliminate-Win, an in-code consistent optional order model that bypasses overhead by moving order management to the application's ordering datalayer. Eliminate-Win uses a token-based algorithm, where requests without observable changes are removed from those observable by at least one other, thus saving network bandwidth and reducing application logic requirements for consistency. We have used Eliminate-Win, an implementation in the Redis enterprise database, and evaluated it against other known solutions in a high-load environment, proving its effectiveness as an efficient, scalable approach to managing RDBMS data integrity.

The results indicate that the sample comprises two distinct sub-populations, potentially stemming from different classes of X-ray binary systems: (1) soft X-ray transients (SXTs) within the Sagittarius A* complex, characterized largely by similar spectral properties and short $\tau$ durations (typically $<1$ yr), likely associated with typical low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs); and (2) a group consisting of SGT sources (soft X-ray giant flares) and possibly SGRs (soft gamma repeaters) located very near Galactic Centre, exhibiting much longer $\tau$ timescales (ranging up to decades), likely originating from magnetars or the high-mass X-ray binary (HMXB) population. The traits of the latter group—specifically their extended intervals and potential high-member count—collectively define a previously unrecognized group of dormant X-ray binaries concentrated in the immediate vicinity of Galactic Centre, a cluster that may have significant implications for modeling the dark matter distribution and overall gravitational potential of the region.

When a massive amount of mass ejection occurs during a stellar outburst, the resulting supersonic flow generates an outward-moving shock wave. This research utilizes one-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations to analyze the conditions leading to such shocks, focusing on how the initial blast pressure determines the shock's ultimate reach, while the self-regulating nature of the subsequent flow controls the internal pressure and timing. A key mechanism identified is envelope heating caused by shocks; this process raises the post-shock state above the stellar's escape velocity, effectively restricting shocks to cases where initial pressure levels are sufficiently intense yet adhering to specific physical laws regarding energy propagation timescales, including a power relationship between initial pressure and shock penetration depth. Furthermore, when the initial outburst pressure exceeds a specific threshold, a layer forms behind the primary shock that expands into space rather than remaining bound to the star, creating an unbounded blastwave capable of stripping substantial mass from a stellar surface.

Notably, by manipulating the relative arrangement of the surfaces and adjusting the phonon parameters, one can dynamically regulate both electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions, a capability with significant implications for optimizing energy efficiency in vibronically assisted charge transport and manipulating spin states via phonon baths to achieve self-sustained electron spins.

Recent advancements in Natural Language Inference (NLI) have benefited significantly from semantic variety in training data; however, its application remains unexplored within fair and transparent benchmarking for NLI datasets. To investigate this area, we present "MultiSemBN," a method that quantifies semantic variety in corpora using one sample from the Bootstrap Nearest Neighbor approach. We applied this methodology to evaluate prominent English and multilingual NLI datasets. The results demonstrate that both English and multilingual NLI training datasets exhibit increased nearest sample bootstrap fractions—indicating higher semantic variety—relative to standalone paragraphs or other multilingual corpus components. In contrast, English and multilingual test sets score lower in semantic variety metrics relative to their respective training sets. Transparency is crucial for the progress of benchmarking in natural language processing, especially as NLI datasets serve as a primary resource for evaluating model capabilities in general text processing. Enhancing transparency and assessing corpus diversity are vital steps toward advancing the field, with NLI benchmarks serving as a key enabler for understanding model proficiency in processing general documents. Our work offers practical approaches to evaluate diversity within natural language corpora by using NLI to benchmark English and multilingual data. We employed a test-sample estimation strategy via the bootstrap nearest neighbor method to measure semantic variety. Investigations into leading English and multilingual NLI datasets reveal high diversity in their training sets compared to test sets, underscoring the disparity needed for transparent evaluation.

Unplanned lane changes represent a significant contributor to lane-change-related accidents. To effectively identify and mitigate these dangerous events, our approach utilizes deep spatiotemporal video analysis to detect hazardous lane-change actions prior to occurrence, thereby supporting proactive driver assistance. This method analyzes short 360° panoramic video clips, processing only relevant regions corresponding to specific road segments to preserve computational efficiency. Spatial analysis is achieved through a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), while temporal dynamics are captured by a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN). This architecture operates on spatial segmentation masks that isolate drivers and adjacent scene areas within the 360° view; however, since standard segmentation techniques are ineffective for unseen video data, our solution adaptively refines these masks dynamically during training using content-based parameters to handle new content reliably. Empirical results demonstrate that this proposed framework delivers high-performing hazardous action detection.

Incremental Learning (IL) requires models to continuously learn from new data streams. A significant IL subset, Class Incremental Learning (CIL), presents a dual challenge: the need to integrate new classes while retaining old knowledge, and the imbalance of class frequencies in the incoming streams. Concerning CIL, most research assumes uniform distribution across classes; however, this study addresses CIL specifically through an imbalanced lens. The paper evaluates multiple strategies for mitigating imbalance effects in CIL, focusing on representation alignment, contrastive learning, and distribution normalization. Ultimately, the authors provide the first comprehensive benchmark for CIL offering a broad spectrum of imbalanced learning solutions. Experimental results indicate that contrastive learning and distribution normalization approaches best enhance model performance regarding both accuracy and imbalance adaptation.

Humans utilize propulsion to advance forward, allowing a single step to cover distance while the other prepares, creating an efficient gait where energy expenditure per meter traveled decreases relative to other durations. Although adding phases like propulsion adds coordination intricacy and potential points of mechanical failure, studies suggest it can significantly lower overall metabolic costs. This research compares level walking and added-step gaits with one or two phases of propulsion across various speeds and heights using a 7-degree-of-freedom humanoid model within a simulation based on minimum work principles. With constraints applied to minimize effort, the results indicate that adding such phases generally reduces work compared to standard gait; furthermore, low-amplitude bouncing during propulsion emerges as a key driver for this efficiency. While both methods offer resilience by requiring comparable work during normal conditions and disruptions, work increases marginally more rapidly following disturbances when propulsion is not utilized. Overall, principles of minimum work confirm that propulsion enhances both efficiency and capacity to recover from disturbances for lower-limb robots, key factors for future unattended home care applications.

This study examines the probability distribution of random matrices where entries follow independent, identically spaced laws, specifically focusing on regimes extending beyond non-intersecting partitions. By leveraging Freidlin's universal local distribution to derive precise results, we address several previously unresolved issues, including the asymptotic behavior of two- and four-marginal distributions, the limit law for the characteristic polynomial, and most notably, the distribution of extreme eigenvalues. We formulate general recommendations for investigating these distributions in other contexts involving independent matrix entries, specifically targeting scenarios outside of non-intersecting partitions.

The recent rapid development of additive manufacturing, specifically two-photon lithography (TPL), enables the precise fabrication of highly intricate periodic acoustic and phononic interfaces at the micro-nano scale. Acoustic metagratings composed of bilaterally symmetric interfaces function similarly to optical gratings but offer a more compact footprint; these units can be engineered to manipulate high-frequency sound waves at microscale dimensions. Achieving this, however, demands exceptional structural accuracy. We present a microacoustic metagrating fabricated via TTPL designed to convert ultrasonic longitudinal waves at 20.6 MHz from one order at a non-zero angle to another order at an equal but opposite angle, leveraging CPL to achieve perfect symmetry in a "super-interface" configuration. By employing an optimized bi-periodic arrangement of interfaces to form a "bi-periodic grating," we achieve simultaneous beam steering for multiple beams at distinct angles. Experimental measurements confirm that this super-structure effectively directs sound at both ~21° and ~79°, aligning closely with theoretical predictions. To the current understanding, this is the first demonstration of a grating-based acoustic device constructed through TPL that operates at an ultra-high frequency of 20.6 MHz, paving the way for the creation of miniature, multifunctional, and complex acoustic devices operating at micro-scales.

Standard normal diffusion, characterized by a linear dependence on time for its mean squared displacement (MSD), often fails to match experiments over significant durations. Specifically, our approach accounts for various temporal behaviors of the permeability, including oscillating or constant effective permeability, and even enables the modeling of un-normal diffusion across multiple temporal ranges before converging to standard diffusion.

Declarative languages like CSP and Lustre enable behavior definition through equations, with compilers automatically generating an efficient executable from this definitions. Finally, we illustrate the technique's application by showing how it is used to develop an efficient interface for a declared workflow management tool.

Multiplexing in spatial mode is identified as a robust technique for robustly detecting early signs of molecular binding events. This method is expected to reliably identify two-photon spatial mode signals at ultra-small scales, enabling sensitive monitoring of occurrence-related data such as that related to individual molecule-binding interfaces.

Bi-timescale ecosystems, such as lakes and forests, are highly susceptible to abrupt, often irreversible transformations. Given the critical necessity of safeguarding their integrity and the biodiversity they sustain, securing sufficient early warning signals for impending regime shifts is vital for effective management and mitigation. This study utilizes time-series data from an aquatic system in Belize to detect such signals within biological structures themselves, a complex undertaking due to data limitations, particularly regarding frequency. We propose a straightforward approach by cross-mapping physiological time-series of individual biological species against simple temperature datasets. The results indicate this method can identify warning signs at least one temperature unit (approx. 10 days or longer) prior to a significant shift. These findings offer a practical, accessible strategy to protect bi-timescale ecosystems by integrating monitoring of physical parameters with basic statistical analysis of biological time-series.

Visual association detection involves confirming whether an image depicts two entities interacting, a task that visual object recognition experts utilize to significantly advance public trust. This work examines the source of inaccuracies in existing association models by analyzing positives that occur spontaneously in training data. To do so, the study introduces a benchmark containing over ten thousand spontaneously occurring pairings extracted from standard association datasets. The authors also investigate the performance of current association detectors on this collection, observing that association models frequently flag these spontaneous instances. By assessing the detector capacity on this specific subset, the research reveals models reaching object classification accuracy. The authors note that while this specific subgroup constitutes a minor fraction of the total dataset, it hinders the ability to associate objects confidently. In response to these insights, the study proposes two practical strategies designed to verify the authenticity of detected pairing and enhance overall accuracy on this challenge.

Dim-light, constrained-data, and real-world action recognition present significant challenges due to hardware and environmental factors that affect sensor performance, as current deep learning models demand large, balanced datasets that are often unavailable in these contexts. We propose a solution combining delta sampling with transfer learning to address sampling-rate disparities and domain shifts between high- and low-fidelity data. By applying transfer learning strategies to source models such as R-BERT, our method adapts these networks to process both original and downsampled inputs, eliminating the need for extensive training on both data types. This approach requires training only the target model using the low-fidelity action datasets, while experiments confirm that our trained R-R-BERT with these conditions matches or exceeds the performance of other transferred models like Kinetics-400 when using limited data.

We examine a specific robust galaxy cluster formed at redshift $z \approx 2.4$, utilizing deep near-infrared imaging and spectroscopy. The target most massive galaxy (the brightest cluster galaxy or BCG) exhibits a distinct two-part structure: a central classical bulge composed largely of old stars showing signs of radial chemical enrichment, and an expansive uneven disk characterized by star-forming spiral arms that wind outward from a central bar. This disk component has a dynamic mass of approximately $4 \times 10^{11} \, \mathrm{M}_{\odot}$—significantly outshining the classical bulge's dynamic mass of roughly $1 \times 10^{11} \, \mathrm{M}_{\odot}$—and spans a diameter near $140 \, \mathrm{M}_{\odot}$. The bulge and disk components are chemically and structurally separate, implying minimal intermingling since their formation. We postulate an external gas accretion event triggered by a merger roughly 900 million years ago, which would have simultaneously induced the development of the inner bar (or enhancement of an existing one) and triggered a burst of internal star formation in the disk region. This scenario offers compelling evidence that both external gas ingestion and internal star-forming processes can drive both the emergence of bar structures and the creation of classical bulges in massive galaxies during the early stages of cosmic history.

The flavor texture hypothesis posits that nature favors simpler structures, suggesting that the global texture zero model—with only ten texture zero parameters—could correctly identify all fundamental quarks and leptons. To rigorously test this model, we implemented a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCKMC) algorithm that systematically scans the permissible parameter space. By systematically evaluating the model's capacity to accommodate observed particle masses and their underlying CP phases, we determined a probable confidence interval for each of the ten parameters. Silicon remains an unmatched leader in the semiconductor industry, yet it faces rising pressure from growing data demands. One pathway to overcome these challenges lies in leveraging electrons' "valley" freedom within silicon, enabling the encoding of two bits per electron compared to a single conventional bit. This capability could drive significant miniaturization in chip design, provided that silicon chips can integrate high-density valleys between electrons, which is essential for the future of ultra-dense memory and processing. Researchers suspect that tailored organic molecules connecting atoms on silicon surfaces facilitate this interaction, but this theory requires validation at an individual scale to enable integration into nanochips. Our study demonstrates exactly this: using a Molecule Break Junction (MBJ), we prove that placing two valley states between two silicon atoms induces interaction between the self-contained atomic electrons' spins, observable through a shift in the current's magnetic sensitivity. Furthermore, because every functional element of a computer ultimately relies on spin-tunneling events, our findings offer foundational knowledge and potential new surface designs for building the ultra-small value state bits required to expand computing and storage capacities beyond current limits, all while utilizing established industrial techniques.

This framework trains incrementally with gradually increasing loss functions to add anatomical plausibility to the defects superimposed on normal brain imagery. Quantum nonlocality represents an intrinsic characteristic of entangled pairs that can be highlighted within various scenarios as "superquantum" or robust forms. Previous research has confirmed such reliable nonlocality for certain nonorthogonal states and specific measurement configurations, yet it remains unknown whether every nonlocal unextendable product basis (UPB) exhibits this robustness. We demonstrate that within the quantum theories possessing commutative or purely noncommutative operator algebras—covering a wide range of reliable cases—it suffices to prove nonlocality only under projective measurements and identical preparations to establish results applicable to all possible realizations concerning a given UPB. By leveraging this framework, we show indeed in any alternative algebraic representation, a particular UPB proven nonlocal in the standard quantic setting yields strong quantum Bell inequality violations and constitutes a quantum pseudoterm for any alternative representation, thereby ensuring robust nonlocality. Further developments include demonstrating such properties for specific UPBs within various alternative algebras and exploring the connection between the algebraic criteria and the concept of quantum pseudo-operators to advance theoretical understanding. Consequently, our work offers both algebraic-based proofs of nonlocality and methods to explore further phenomena associated with reliable nonlocality.

Line connections in digital road maps serve as a significant source of visual information, yet high-density clustering frequently induces spatial anti-aliasing artifacts that severely impair driving experience and navigation quality. Secondly, targeting spatial anti-aliasing specifically, we introduce a new rendering technique featuring a variable number of segments and dynamic gap widths. This gap-based approach replaces traditional methods using multiple parallel lines, utilizing spatial calculation formulas to derive distribution parameters for each line. Results indicate a substantial reduction in visual interference and anti-aliasing effects both within line groups and at their boundaries, significantly enhancing the overall visualization and driving information quality of digital road maps.

Structural polarization represents a critical issue in public policy and political science. Yet, current structural polarization measures remain under-developed, lacking the statistical rigor necessary for robust analytical frameworks. This paper examines existing metrics, identifies emerging methodologies applicable to longitudinal policy analysis, and proposes new, standardized measures. Specifically, we introduce the Minimum Coalitional Coalition (MCC) index to quantify coalition formation within legislative bodies, as well as the Number of Majority Coalitions (NUMJ), defined as a count variable, to track bipartisan legislation frequency over time. Utilizing congressional roll call data, we apply these metrics to demonstrate their efficacy in capturing polarization distinctively from party distinctiveness. Furthermore, we highlight the significance of standardization in ensuring these tools function as reliable assets for the political science research community.

Navigating urban roads often prompts drivers to consult navigation services for suggestions that minimize travel time or avoid traffic congestion. Building on the concept of using probe vehicles to estimate queue lengths, this paper introduces a simple, cost-effective design for collecting relevant data. Under suitable assumptions about the underlying queue dynamics and probe vehicle distribution, the proposed estimator is demonstrated to be consistent and asymptotically normal. Finally, applied to real-world data from a traffic queue in Washington, D.C., an actual implementation of the estimator is presented along with associated simulations.

The fundamental principles governing the thermoelectric responses of chiral magnetic materials remain largely uncharted. Recently, a hypothesis suggested that a Casimir force-like effect underpins the anomalous Nernst and magneto-Seebeck phenomena seen in chiral metallic structures; according to this view, they result from the massive screening of Casimir forces. In this study, we measure the electric, magnetic, and field-dependent thermal resistances of a (111)-oriented Mn$_3$NiN monolayer. The results reveal that both the electric and thermal Hall coefficients—along with the Nernst effect—exhibit pronounced oscillations with varying external field orientations. These large Hall responses correlate directly with the oscillations in the longitudinal Seebeck coefficient and Nernst efficiency. Furthermore, by seeing these phenomena tie into thermal properties, we suggest a unified framework to understand the complex thermal and electrical Hall responses inherent to black-hole-like materials.

Quantum annealing emerges as a viable strategy for optimizing complex landscapes, particularly when the Hamiltonian adheres to Stoquastic constraints, where the $Z$-basis terms are real and non-negative. Decoherence, however, can detrimentally impact its performance when these terms are complex. We demonstrate that even a solitary complex component within the target Hamiltonian can cause a complete breakdown of quantum annealing. In its presence, the system evolves toward a trivial state that fails to match the ground state, effectively replacing smooth adiabatic progression with an abrupt sudden transition. The study reveals that quantum superpositions inherent in the Hamiltonian's time-dependent form generate large energy gaps, causing the adiabatic protocol to collapse; furthermore, the Fidelity between the eventual state and the intended ground state drops below 1 due to the initial Hamiltonian's specific structure. Nevertheless, natural environmental decoherence can mitigate this issue, potentially restoring performance. The outcomes indicate a distinct class of Hamiltonian forms and suggest that accounting for decoherence may assist in selecting suitable problems suited for quantum annealing approaches.

This work examines the convergence behavior of a model-parallel training architecture for artificial neural networks, where only weight updates are exchanged between an originating node and various model-evaluation regions corresponding to specific layer groups. By leveraging convergence characteristics standard for fully distributed training, we derive convergence rates for this partitioned scheme, assuming the weight exchange frequency functions as either a constant or a stochastic sequence tied primarily to a nonexchangeable mixing rate within the system. Our findings confirm full model convergence even when parameter updates occur at sparse intervals; this approach likely mitigates the stability concerns often associated with high-frequency inter-node communication. In conjunction with existing methods addressing bit-width reductions or encoder-transmission strategy optimizations, the capability for reduced update frequency presents a promising avenue for expanding neural network layer depth. Numerical results align well with the proposed theoretical frameworks.

This study investigates harmonic (contour) arrangement within fiber-reinforced polymer composites designed for structural health monitoring, evaluated via Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT). A dual-objective evolutionary algorithm was implemented to extract exact harmonic coordinates from experimental EIT datasets. Impedance measurements revealed distinct signal patterns corresponding to true harmonic positions; however, EIT reconstructions typically yielded only approximate symmetry. By applying the proposed algorithm to actual composite data, the method successfully determined precise harmonic contours, thereby addressing a critical knowledge gap in determining exact harmonic configurations within these materials.

Advanced AI agents are increasingly tasked with solving complex problems, which often requires taming inherently capricious generative models to produce reliable, high-quality outputs—a necessity for maintaining system integrity. We introduce a theoretical framework and practical approaches for adding post-generation reliability to large language models by analyzing the statistical distributions of their outputs. We term the method described here GenStat, which leverages the application of specific post-processing functions to refine linguistic distributions. Central to our methodology is the concept of GenCost, a quantitative metric that assesses the difficulty of generating certain texts, estimated via the collective application of generated solutions. We demonstrate that GenCost effectively predicts and explains both the textual characteristics produced by LLMs and their performance on various natural language tasks. Additionally, we show how GenCost can optimize prompt engineering, parameter configurations, and model selection processes. Empirically, this approach has been tested on datasets of varying difficulty, including those involving image analysis, code execution, and knowledge application. Our results indicate improvements in both precision and recall across all categories, most notably reaching up to 55.8% improvement for harder datasets.

We address the challenge of generalization in reinforcement learning agents by focusing on multi-domain robot learning, specifically extending the Reinforcement Learning with Demons (RLD) approach to batch linear Markov decision processes (MDS). Theoretical bounds for RLD batch linear vector machines demonstrate that, under full observability, the approach can acquire functions in any number of domains using significantly fewer samples per domain when the number of RLDs remains low. Moreover, if the supplied RLD utilizes supplementary information—such as domain similarities derived from reward function regressors—the bounds tighten substantially. Specifically, if sup-domain training data and RLDs utilize $K$ bits per non-supervised parameter, the batch RLD approach guarantees generalization within a factor of approx. 2.83 (or more precisely, related exponential terms) by multiplying standard batch RBS multipliers by an additional factor compared to other methods when evaluated over homogeneous MDS with similar rewards but different RLD configurations. If sup-domain training data and RLD dimensions utilize even larger bit overhead per non-supervised parameter, the bound improves dramatically such that the multiplicative increase becomes roughly proportional to $\exp(2\sqrt{\log KD / \log (2KD)})$ when assessing performance on fully observed MDS instances with reward functions having identical rewards but differing RLD counts.

Model reduction is a well-established technique aimed at creating simplified, usable models derived from high-fidelity dynamic systems. We validate this approach on a standard benchmark from literature, demonstrating a speed increase of approximately 40 times when compared to traditional reduction techniques.

In a rapidly evolving world, continuous learning is increasingly essential. Within this context, an increasing number of individuals are turning to their smartphones to access educational resources. However, an important issue arises when users rely on educational apps for training: the quality of their learning experience depends on the diversity of the content they consume. Unfortunately, users often restrict their engagement to a single source or narrow range of materials, leading to informational cocoons that degrade their overall experience. To solve this challenge and encourage users to explore more diverse content, the paper proposes utilizing random walk algorithms for learning from data distributed in a federated manner. The core objective here is to minimize the discrepancy (measured by KL-divergence error) between a target concept and the actual concepts being learned through a random walk performed in a settings where data remains locally distributed. The results demonstrate that learning from such federated diverse datasets via random walk methods achieve performance nearly equivalent to training on perfectly matched data, while significantly promoting the consumption of varied content by users.

This research examined whether forced therapy improves or maintains the psychological health of incarcerated people. A sample comprising 399 prisoners (63% male, 52% White, average age 34.12 years) participated. Data indicated 80% had undergone mandatory counseling, while the remainder chose to do so voluntarily. Unsupervised and supervised learning approaches remain the primary methods for creating AI models intended to assist radiologists in performing medical image segmentation, even though annotation scarcity is common in the healthcare industry. Although recent advances in consistency regularization have enabled significant progress by leveraging self-supervised pre-trained models and consolidating limited labeled data alongside abundant unlabeled alternatives, these techniques typically encounter obstacles related to implementation, including difficult mathematical formulations, reliance on proprietary tools like Awkward (which hinders integration), and dependence on heuristic parameter tuning for consistency regularization. This paper presents an industry-oriented solution by adapting a popular radiologist-assisted workflow for breast cancer segmentation using 840 annotated and a dataset of approximately 19,000 unannotated images. The implemented method improves AUC performance on the annotated test set from the baseline 61%, achieved by supervised fine-tuning with labeled data, to 64%, and further boosts the score to 67% when enhancing the fine-tuned model with self-supervised techniques using the prepared datasets.
